'''John Dickson Baldeschwieler''' (born 1933) is an American [[chemist]] who has made significant contributions in molecular structure and [[spectroscopy]].

Born on November 14, 1933, in [[Elizabeth, New Jersey]], he was an alumnus of [[Cornell University]] ([[Bachelor of Science|B.S.]], 1956, Chemical Engineering) and the [[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Ph.D.]], 1959).<ref name="thesis-baldeschwieler-1960">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/301871881/ |title=Structure of unstable compounds by matrix isolation techniques |date=1960 |publisher=[[University of California, Berkeley]] |type=Ph.D. |last=Baldeschwieler |first=John Dickson  |id={{ProQuest|301871881 }} |url-access=subscription  |oclc=29101714}}</ref> He has taught at [[Harvard University]], [[Stanford University]] and currently is the J. Stanley Johnson Professor and professor of chemistry, emeritus at [[Caltech]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cce.caltech.edu/content/john-d-baldeschwieler |title=Caltech Division of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering Directory |access-date=2015-04-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180126022427/http://www.cce.caltech.edu/content/john-d-baldeschwieler |archive-date=2018-01-26 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://oralhistories.library.caltech.edu/154/1/Baldeschwieler_OHO.pdf|title=Interview John D. Baldeschwieler archived by Caltech}}</ref><ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= John D. Baldeschwieler |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/baldeschwieler-john-d|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="transcript">{{cite book|first1=David C. |last1=Brock|first2=Arthur |last2=Daemmrich |title=John D. Baldeschwieler, Transcript of an Interviews Conducted by David C. ==Awards and recognition==
Baldeschwieler has received multiple awards for his research, including the [[National Medal of Science]], awarded in 2000, "For his imaginative development of new methods for determining the properties, structures, motions and interactions of molecules and molecular assemblies, the translation of these advances into practical pharmaceutical and instrumentation products for the public benefit, and extensive service to his government and the scientific community."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.jsp?recip_id=28 |title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details}}</ref> He was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 1970, the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 1972 and the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 1979.

Additional awards include:
* 1962–1965  [[Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship]]
* 1967  Award in Pure Chemistry, [[American Chemical Society]]
* 1968  Fresenius Award of [[Phi Lambda Upsilon]]
* 1989  Richard C. Tolman Medal, [[American Chemical Society]]
* 1990  William H. Nichols Medal, [[American Chemical Society]]
* 2001  Award for Creative Invention, [[American Chemical Society]]
* 2003  [[Othmer Gold Medal]], [[Chemical Heritage Foundation]]
